ccu-lesson-01-acs.stem: Which set contains the three presentations of acute coronary syndrome?

choices.text: Unstable angina, NSTEMI, STEMI
choices.explanation: These form the ACS spectrum.

choices.text: Stable angina, sinus bradycardia, CHB
choices.explanation: These are not the three ACS categories.

choices.text: Heart failure, DCM, pulmonary edema
choices.explanation: These describe other cardiac diagnoses or manifestations.

choices.text: PEA, asystole, ventricular fibrillation
choices.explanation: These are arrest rhythms rather than ACS categories.

ccu-lesson-01-acs.point: ACS includes unstable angina, NSTEMI, and STEMI.

ccu-lesson-01-acs.stem: Which distinction separates unstable angina from myocardial infarction?

choices.text: No biomarker evidence of myocardial necrosis
choices.explanation: Ischemia occurs without the myocardial necrosis defining infarction.

choices.text: No coronary blood-flow reduction
choices.explanation: Coronary ischemia remains central to unstable angina.

choices.text: No need for urgent assessment
choices.explanation: Concerning ischemic symptoms still require urgent assessment.

choices.text: No possibility of an abnormal ECG
choices.explanation: Unstable angina can have ischemic ECG changes.

ccu-lesson-01-acs.point: Unstable angina is ischemia without biomarker evidence of necrosis.

ccu-lesson-01-acs.stem: A patient has myocardial infarction without persistent ST elevation. Which category best matches?

choices.text: NSTEMI
choices.explanation: This infarction category lacks persistent ST elevation.

choices.text: Stable angina
choices.explanation: This does not describe established myocardial infarction.

choices.text: Unstable angina
choices.explanation: This lacks the biomarker evidence of necrosis defining MI.

choices.text: Complete heart block
choices.explanation: This is a conduction diagnosis rather than the ACS category.

ccu-lesson-01-acs.point: NSTEMI does not require persistent ST elevation.

ccu-lesson-01-acs.stem: Which presentation most strongly fits the ischemic symptom pattern in ACS?

choices.text: Central chest pressure with sweating and arm radiation
choices.explanation: This is the ischemic symptom cluster.

choices.text: Sharp localized chest pain reproduced by pressing one rib
choices.explanation: This is more suggestive of a chest-wall explanation, although symptoms still need assessment.

choices.text: Burning after a meal with sour regurgitation and no exertional pattern
choices.explanation: This more closely fits a reflux pattern.

choices.text: Brief focal chest discomfort during trunk rotation without systemic symptoms
choices.explanation: This is less characteristic of the ischemic pattern.

ccu-lesson-01-acs.stem: After initial assessment of suspected ACS, which test most directly provides electrical evidence used to guide urgent treatment?

choices.text: Diagnostic 12-lead ECG
choices.explanation: It supplies the electrical views needed to identify ischemic patterns.

choices.text: Continuous pulse-oximeter pleth recording
choices.explanation: It measures pulsatile flow and oxygenation rather than ischemic electrical views.

choices.text: Serial noninvasive BP recording
choices.explanation: This assesses hemodynamics rather than myocardial electrical patterns.

choices.text: Initial serum electrolyte measurement
choices.explanation: Electrolytes inform assessment but do not provide a diagnostic electrical tracing.

ccu-lesson-01-acs.point: Initial ACS assessment includes vitals, monitoring, prompt ECG, access, and escalation.

ccu-lesson-01-acs.stem: A patient with suspected ACS has adequate oxygenation and no respiratory distress. Which factor should determine supplemental oxygen use?

choices.text: Evidence of an oxygenation or clinical need under the protocol
choices.explanation: Oxygen should be given when clinically indicated.

choices.text: The ACS diagnosis regardless of oxygenation
choices.explanation: The diagnosis alone is not the stated indication.

choices.text: The severity of pain regardless of oxygenation
choices.explanation: Pain severity does not itself establish a need for oxygen.

choices.text: The presence of ST elevation regardless of oxygenation
choices.explanation: ST elevation requires urgent care but does not itself establish hypoxemia.

ccu-lesson-01-acs.point: Use oxygen when oxygenation or clinical status indicates it.

ccu-lesson-01-acs.stem: Chest pressure persists with new ischemic ECG changes and a falling BP. The first troponin result is pending. Which action has priority?

choices.text: Escalate immediately while continuing assessment and monitoring
choices.explanation: Instability and ischemic findings should not wait for a biomarker result.

choices.text: Schedule a repeat pain score after the routine round
choices.explanation: This delays action despite deterioration.

choices.text: Complete the dietary history before contacting the team
choices.explanation: This is secondary to urgent assessment and escalation.

choices.text: Wait for the biomarker result before reporting the ECG
choices.explanation: This delay can postpone urgent assessment and treatment.

ccu-lesson-01-acs.point: Do not delay escalation of concerning ischemia while awaiting biomarkers.

ccu-lesson-01-acs.stem: A patient has ongoing ischemic chest pain and compatible new ST elevation. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

choices.text: A time-critical ACS presentation needing urgent escalation
choices.explanation: Clinical and ECG findings support immediate action; a biomarker delay is unsafe.

choices.text: A normal telemetry variant because pain is present
choices.explanation: Pain does not make the ECG finding benign.

choices.text: A diagnosis of stable exertional angina established by symptoms
choices.explanation: Persistent acute symptoms and compatible ST elevation require a different response.

choices.text: A reason to defer assessment until pain resolves
choices.explanation: Waiting can delay time-sensitive care.

ccu-lesson-01-acs.point: An acute ischemic presentation with ST elevation needs urgent assessment.

ccu-lesson-01-acs.stem: What is the immediate physiological problem in ACS?

choices.text: Reduced coronary supply causing myocardial ischemia
choices.explanation: This is the central supply problem.

choices.text: Reduced systemic venous return as the defining mechanism
choices.explanation: This does not define ACS.

choices.text: Primary AV conduction failure without ischemia
choices.explanation: This defines a different problem.

choices.text: Primary ventricular repolarization delay without ischemia
choices.explanation: This does not define ACS.

ccu-lesson-01-acs.point: Reduced coronary blood flow produces acute myocardial ischemia.

choices.text: Failure of atrial impulses to conduct to the ventricles
choices.explanation: Atria and ventricles then beat independently.

choices.text: Uniformly slow sinus impulses that all conduct
choices.explanation: This describes sinus bradycardia rather than complete block.

choices.text: Rapid conduction through every atrial impulse
choices.explanation: This does not describe AV dissociation.

choices.text: A ventricular rate that must exceed the atrial rate
choices.explanation: This is not the defining relationship.

ccu-lesson-02-chb.point: Third-degree AV block produces independent atrial and ventricular activity.

ccu-lesson-02-chb.stem: Which tracing relationship most supports CHB?

choices.text: P waves and QRS complexes with no fixed PR relationship
choices.explanation: Independent atrial and ventricular rhythms are the hallmark.

choices.text: Each P wave followed by one QRS with a fixed PR
choices.explanation: This demonstrates conducted atrial impulses rather than complete block.

choices.text: A continuous absence of all atrial and ventricular signals
choices.explanation: That does not describe an atrial rhythm with a ventricular escape.

choices.text: A normal P/QRS relationship with a fast sinus rate
choices.explanation: This is not complete AV block.

ccu-lesson-02-chb.stem: Which complication explains dizziness and hypotension during severe CHB?

choices.text: Reduced cardiac output from a slow ventricular escape
choices.explanation: Inadequate effective rate can impair perfusion.

choices.text: Increased coronary flow from faster AV conduction
choices.explanation: Complete block prevents normal AV conduction.

choices.text: Increased ventilation from atrial dissociation alone
choices.explanation: This does not explain the hemodynamic problem.

choices.text: Reduced platelet aggregation from the escape rhythm
choices.explanation: The rhythm does not act as an antiplatelet.

ccu-lesson-02-chb.point: A slow escape rhythm can reduce output and organ perfusion.

ccu-lesson-02-chb.stem: Two patients have a ventricular rate of 38/min. One has fixed P-to-QRS conduction; the other has independent P and QRS rhythms. Which distinction is valid?

choices.text: The conduction relationship, not rate alone, separates the patterns
choices.explanation: Complete block has AV dissociation; sinus bradycardia preserves conduction.

choices.text: The identical rates establish the same rhythm diagnosis
choices.explanation: Rate alone is insufficient.

choices.text: A narrow QRS excludes AV dissociation
choices.explanation: QRS width alone does not establish the P/QRS relationship.

choices.text: A palpable pulse excludes complete block
choices.explanation: A ventricular escape can produce a pulse despite complete block.

ccu-lesson-02-chb.point: Sinus bradycardia preserves conducted P/QRS relationships.

ccu-lesson-02-chb.stem: Which recent treatment is a plausible contributor to AV conduction slowing in CHB assessment?

choices.text: A beta-blocker or AV-node-slowing calcium-channel blocker
choices.explanation: These are named medication contributors.

choices.text: An oral local antifungal alone
choices.explanation: This is not a principal AV-node-slowing medicine.

choices.text: A vitamin supplement alone
choices.explanation: This is not the medication contributor.

choices.text: An osmotic laxative alone
choices.explanation: This is not a direct AV-node-slowing therapy.

ccu-lesson-02-chb.point: Review reversible contributors including rate-slowing medicines and electrolyte problems.

ccu-lesson-02-chb.stem: A patient with AV dissociation has a slow pulse, confusion, and hypotension. Which treatment capability should the nurse prepare with the urgent team?

choices.text: Pacing support
choices.explanation: The patient has dangerous symptomatic bradycardia with poor perfusion.

choices.text: Routine synchronized treatment of a fast rhythm
choices.explanation: The dominant problem is severe bradycardia.

choices.text: A maintenance oral antihypertensive alone
choices.explanation: This does not address the low-output conduction emergency.

choices.text: A routine discharge ECG alone
choices.explanation: The unstable presentation requires immediate escalation.

ccu-lesson-02-chb.point: Escalate symptomatic CHB and prepare for pacing.

ccu-lesson-02-chb.stem: A monitor suggests CHB while the patient is awake. What determines the urgency of the bedside response?

choices.text: Pulse, BP, consciousness, breathing, and symptoms
choices.explanation: The rhythm must be interpreted with the patient’s clinical state.

choices.text: The diagnostic label without a patient assessment
choices.explanation: The label alone does not quantify current perfusion.

choices.text: The monitor’s alarm volume alone
choices.explanation: Alarm volume is a device setting.

choices.text: The time since the last routine meal alone
choices.explanation: Meal timing does not establish hemodynamic stability.

ccu-lesson-02-chb.point: Correlate a conduction pattern with the patient’s perfusion.

ccu-lesson-02-chb.stem: A patient with new CHB has worsening hypoxemia and high potassium. Which interpretation should inform escalation?

choices.text: Both findings can contribute and need urgent review alongside the block
choices.explanation: Hypoxia and hyperkalemia are named contributors.

choices.text: Neither finding matters once complete block is identified
choices.explanation: Reversible contributors still require assessment.

choices.text: High potassium establishes that oxygenation no longer matters
choices.explanation: Both physiological problems remain relevant.

choices.text: A palpable escape pulse establishes that both abnormalities are harmless
choices.explanation: A pulse does not guarantee adequate perfusion or safety.

ccu-lesson-02-chb.point: Hypoxia and hyperkalemia are reversible contributors to conduction deterioration.

ccu-lesson-03-12lead-ecg.point: A diagnostic 12-lead ECG uses ten physical electrodes.
ccu-lesson-03-12lead-ecg.stem: How many physical electrodes are used for a standard 12-lead ECG? Enter a whole number.
ccu-lesson-03-12lead-ecg.explanation: Four limb and six chest electrodes provide ten physical contacts.

ccu-lesson-03-12lead-ecg.stem: Which distinction correctly separates electrode and lead?

choices.text: Electrode: physical contact; lead: electrical view
choices.explanation: The machine derives views from the physical contacts.

choices.text: Electrode: electrical view; lead: physical sticker
choices.explanation: This reverses the terms.

choices.text: Electrode: pulse-oximeter wave; lead: oxygen saturation
choices.explanation: These refer to a different monitoring signal.

choices.text: Electrode: ventricular contraction; lead: arterial pulse
choices.explanation: Neither definition matches ECG terminology.

ccu-lesson-03-12lead-ecg.point: An electrode is a physical contact; a lead is an electrical view.

choices.text: 4th intercostal space, right sternal border

choices.text: At V4’s horizontal level, anterior axillary line
choices.explanation: This is the V5 position.

choices.text: 4th intercostal space, right sternal border

choices.text: 4th intercostal space, right sternal border
choices.explanation: This is the V1 position, not V6.

choices.text: 4th intercostal space, left sternal border
choices.explanation: This is the V2 position, not V6.

choices.text: Halfway between V2 and V4
choices.explanation: This is the V3 position, not V6.

ccu-lesson-03-12lead-ecg.stem: Which event is represented by the P wave?

choices.text: Atrial depolarization
choices.explanation: This is the electrical event associated with the P wave.

choices.text: Ventricular depolarization
choices.explanation: This is not the electrical event represented by the P wave.

choices.text: Ventricular repolarization
choices.explanation: This is not the electrical event represented by the P wave.

choices.text: Mechanical ventricular ejection
choices.explanation: This is not the electrical event represented by the P wave.

ccu-lesson-03-12lead-ecg.stem: Which event is represented by the QRS complex?

choices.text: Ventricular depolarization
choices.explanation: This is the electrical event associated with the QRS complex.

choices.text: Atrial depolarization
choices.explanation: This is not the electrical event represented by the QRS complex.

choices.text: Ventricular repolarization
choices.explanation: This is not the electrical event represented by the QRS complex.

choices.text: Mechanical ventricular ejection
choices.explanation: This is not the electrical event represented by the QRS complex.

ccu-lesson-03-12lead-ecg.stem: Which event is represented by the T wave?

choices.text: Ventricular repolarization
choices.explanation: This is the electrical event associated with the T wave.

choices.text: Atrial depolarization
choices.explanation: This is not the electrical event represented by the T wave.

choices.text: Ventricular depolarization
choices.explanation: This is not the electrical event represented by the T wave.

choices.text: Mechanical ventricular ejection
choices.explanation: This is not the electrical event represented by the T wave.

choices.text: Red
choices.explanation: This is a different IEC limb-electrode color.

choices.text: Green

ccu-lesson-03-12lead-ecg.stem: In the IEC color system, what color is LL/F?

choices.explanation: This is the specified IEC color for LL/F.

choices.text: Yellow

choices.text: Black
choices.explanation: This is a different IEC limb-electrode color.

ccu-lesson-03-12lead-ecg.stem: In the IEC color system, what color is RL/N?

choices.text: Black
choices.explanation: This is the specified IEC color for RL/N.

choices.text: Red

choices.explanation: This is a different IEC limb-electrode color.

ccu-lesson-03-12lead-ecg.stem: V1 and V2 were placed above the fourth intercostal space, and the tracing now appears unexpectedly abnormal. Which technical issue should be corrected before interpreting a stable patient’s repeat ECG?

choices.text: Chest-electrode position
choices.explanation: High V1/V2 placement can distort the tracing.

choices.text: The number of electrical leads selected alone
choices.explanation: A standard lead display does not correct misplaced electrodes.

choices.text: The pulse-oximeter’s display brightness
choices.explanation: That does not correct an ECG electrode-position error.

choices.text: The oxygen tubing length alone
choices.explanation: That does not determine chest-electrode anatomy.

ccu-lesson-03-12lead-ecg.point: High V1/V2 placement can produce a misleading tracing.

ccu-lesson-03-12lead-ecg.stem: V4 is correctly located. What determines the vertical level of V5 and V6?

choices.text: The same horizontal level as V4
choices.explanation: Their axillary positions share V4’s level.

choices.text: The same vertical line as V1
choices.explanation: The sternal V1 position does not set their axillary placement.

choices.text: One intercostal space above V4
choices.explanation: This is not the level.

choices.text: One intercostal space below V4
choices.explanation: This is not the level.

ccu-lesson-03-12lead-ecg.point: V5 and V6 share V4’s horizontal level.

ccu-lesson-03-12lead-ecg.stem: A patient asks why twelve electrical views do not require twelve stickers. Which explanation is correct?

choices.text: Leads are derived views rather than one sticker per view
choices.explanation: Four limb plus six chest contacts provide the standard derived leads.

choices.text: Two chest electrodes are omitted in a routine recording
choices.explanation: A standard recording still uses six chest electrodes.

choices.text: The pleth trace supplies the two missing electrical leads
choices.explanation: A pulse-oximeter waveform is not an ECG lead.

choices.text: Two stickers are counted twice because they are spares
choices.explanation: Spare contacts do not explain the derived lead system.

ccu-lesson-03-12lead-ecg.point: Ten electrodes can generate twelve derived views.

ccu-lesson-03-12lead-ecg.stem: In the IEC limb labels, what do F and N mean?

choices.text: F: Foot; N: Neutral
choices.explanation: These identify the stated foot and neutral labels.

choices.text: F: Front; N: Neck
choices.explanation: These are not the stated IEC label meanings.

choices.text: F: Frequency; N: Node
choices.explanation: These are not the stated limb label meanings.

choices.text: F: Filter; N: Negative
choices.explanation: These are not the stated limb label meanings.

ccu-lesson-03-12lead-ecg.point: In IEC limb labels F means Foot and N means Neutral.

ccu-lesson-04-telemetry.stem: What is the principal role of telemetry?

choices.text: Continuous cardiac electrical rhythm monitoring
choices.explanation: Telemetry follows heart rate and rhythm over time.

choices.text: Replacement of every diagnostic 12-lead assessment
choices.explanation: Continuous rhythm monitoring does not provide the same diagnostic study.

choices.text: Direct measurement of myocardial blood flow
choices.explanation: Telemetry measures electrical activity rather than coronary flow.

choices.text: Direct measurement of cardiac output
choices.explanation: The ECG waveform does not directly quantify output.

ccu-lesson-04-telemetry.point: Telemetry monitoring and diagnostic 12-lead ECG have different roles.

ccu-lesson-04-telemetry.stem: Which pairing correctly identifies the signals?

choices.text: ECG: electrical activity; pleth: pulsatile blood flow
choices.explanation: ECG electrodes and an oximeter probe measure different signals.

choices.text: ECG: arterial oxygen content; pleth: AV conduction
choices.explanation: This reverses and misidentifies the signal roles.

choices.text: ECG: urine output; pleth: coronary anatomy
choices.explanation: Neither definition fits.

choices.text: ECG: ventricular pressure; pleth: clotting intensity
choices.explanation: These are not what the waveforms directly measure.

ccu-lesson-04-telemetry.point: ECG and pleth arise from different physiological signals.

ccu-lesson-04-telemetry.stem: After looking at the patient, which set belongs in systematic rhythm interpretation?

choices.text: Rate, regularity, P waves, PR, QRS, and P/QRS relationship
choices.explanation: These are the ECG features.

choices.text: Blood group, INR, platelet count, and bilirubin
choices.explanation: These are not the systematic rhythm sequence.

choices.text: Pain score, wound depth, and drainage volume
choices.explanation: These assess another clinical domain.

choices.text: Bowel frequency, dietary intake, and stool color
choices.explanation: These do not interpret cardiac electrical relationships.

ccu-lesson-04-telemetry.point: Interpret rate and intervals with the patient and P/QRS relationship.
Estimate rate from a six-second strip.
ccu-lesson-04-telemetry.stem: A six-second ECG strip contains 9 QRS complexes. What is the approximate heart rate?
ccu-lesson-04-telemetry.explanation: Multiply the six-second QRS count by ten.

ccu-lesson-04-telemetry.point: Use the 300 method only for a regular rhythm.
ccu-lesson-04-telemetry.stem: A regular rhythm has 4 large boxes between successive R waves on an ECG recorded at 25 mm/s. Estimate the heart rate in beats/min.
ccu-lesson-04-telemetry.explanation: For a regular rhythm, 300 divided by 4 equals 75.

ccu-lesson-04-telemetry.stem: Which pair falls within the usual reference limits for the PR interval and QRS duration?

choices.text: PR 0.16 s; QRS 0.08 s
choices.explanation: PR is about 0.12–0.20 s and QRS less than 0.12 s.

choices.text: PR 0.28 s; QRS 0.16 s
choices.explanation: Both are outside the stated normal limits.

choices.text: PR 0.32 s; QRS 0.18 s
choices.explanation: These are prolonged rather than the normal pair.

choices.text: PR 0.26 s; QRS 0.14 s
choices.explanation: These exceed the stated reference intervals.

ccu-lesson-04-telemetry.point: Recognize the taught normal PR and QRS intervals.

ccu-lesson-04-telemetry.stem: The monitor appears chaotic, but the patient is talking and has a strong regular pulse. Which explanation should be assessed first?

choices.text: Artifact or lead-related signal disturbance
choices.explanation: The electrical display conflicts with the observed perfusing patient.

choices.text: Established pulseless ventricular fibrillation
choices.explanation: The patient has a definite regular pulse and is responsive.

choices.text: Established asystole
choices.explanation: A talking patient with a regular pulse is not described as asystolic.

choices.text: Established pulseless electrical activity
choices.explanation: A definite pulse contradicts PEA.

ccu-lesson-04-telemetry.point: Assess the patient and pulse when a tracing may be artifact.

ccu-lesson-04-telemetry.stem: A patient has a regular pleth waveform and new ischemic chest pain. Which investigation is still needed to assess ischemic electrical changes?

choices.text: A diagnostic 12-lead ECG
choices.explanation: Pleth does not provide diagnostic electrical views.

choices.text: A longer pleth recording
choices.explanation: This still measures pulsatile flow rather than ischemic electrical activity.

choices.text: A repeat oxygen-saturation measurement
choices.explanation: Oxygenation alone cannot characterize ischemic ECG changes.

choices.text: A repeat peripheral pulse-rate count
choices.explanation: Rate alone does not provide ischemic electrical views.

ccu-lesson-04-telemetry.point: A pleth pulse signal does not replace a diagnostic ECG.
A common basic telemetry setup uses three electrodes.
ccu-lesson-04-telemetry.stem: How many electrodes are used for standard three-lead telemetry?
ccu-lesson-04-telemetry.explanation: Three-lead telemetry uses three electrodes for continuous rhythm monitoring.

ccu-lesson-05-dangerous-rhythms.stem: Which pair is shockable in cardiac arrest?

choices.text: Ventricular fibrillation and pulseless VT
choices.explanation: Both follow the shockable arrest pathway.

choices.text: Asystole and PEA
choices.explanation: These are non-shockable arrest rhythms.

choices.text: Sinus bradycardia and CHB with a pulse
choices.explanation: These are pulse-present bradycardia problems.

choices.text: Stable sinus tachycardia and normal sinus rhythm
choices.explanation: These are not shockable arrest rhythms.

ccu-lesson-05-dangerous-rhythms.point: VF and pulseless VT are shockable arrest rhythms.

ccu-lesson-05-dangerous-rhythms.stem: Which pair belongs to the non-shockable arrest pathway?

choices.text: PEA and asystole
choices.explanation: They require CPR, indicated medicines, and cause-directed treatment, not routine defibrillation.

choices.text: VF and pulseless VT
choices.explanation: These belong to the shockable pathway.

choices.text: Unstable regular SVT and atrial flutter with a pulse
choices.explanation: These are pulse-present tachyarrhythmia contexts.

choices.text: Sinus bradycardia and a perfusing ventricular escape
choices.explanation: These are not defined here as pulseless arrest.

ccu-lesson-05-dangerous-rhythms.point: PEA and asystole are non-shockable arrest rhythms.

choices.text: Organized electrical activity without a pulse
choices.explanation: PEA is a clinical electrical–mechanical mismatch, not one specific tracing shape.

choices.text: A rapid rhythm with a strong pulse
choices.explanation: A pulse excludes the definition of PEA.

choices.text: A slow rhythm with normal BP
choices.explanation: This is a perfusing rhythm.

choices.text: A pleth trace with a normal ECG
choices.explanation: This does not define PEA.

ccu-lesson-05-dangerous-rhythms.point: PEA is electrical activity without a palpable pulse.

ccu-lesson-05-dangerous-rhythms.stem: A wide-complex tachycardia appears. Which bedside assessment first separates the arrest pathway from the pulse-present tachyarrhythmia pathway?

choices.text: A definite pulse
choices.explanation: Pulse status determines this initial pathway distinction.

choices.text: The degree of hypotension
choices.explanation: This helps assess instability after a pulse is confirmed.

choices.text: The severity of chest discomfort
choices.explanation: This helps assess instability but does not establish whether a pulse is present.

choices.text: The presence of acute pulmonary edema
choices.explanation: This indicates compromise but does not replace the pulse check.

ccu-lesson-05-dangerous-rhythms.point: Pulse status separates pulseless VT from pulse-present VT management.

ccu-lesson-05-dangerous-rhythms.stem: A patient with tachycardia has hypotension and acute confusion. Which interpretation best fits?

choices.text: Hemodynamic instability
choices.explanation: The perfusion findings determine urgency alongside the rhythm.

choices.text: Stability established by a regular rhythm
choices.explanation: Regularity does not exclude poor perfusion.

choices.text: Stability established by a narrow QRS
choices.explanation: QRS width does not establish adequate circulation.

choices.text: A harmless rhythm established by a previous similar episode
choices.explanation: Prior episodes do not determine the present clinical state.

ccu-lesson-05-dangerous-rhythms.point: Hypotension, altered consciousness, shock, ischemia, or acute HF indicates instability.

ccu-lesson-05-dangerous-rhythms.stem: An unresponsive patient has organized ECG activity, no normal breathing, and no definite pulse. Which pathway fits?

choices.text: The non-shockable cardiac-arrest pathway
choices.explanation: Organized electrical activity without a pulse is PEA.

choices.text: Observation for an asymptomatic perfusing rhythm
choices.explanation: The patient is unresponsive and pulseless.

choices.text: Routine oral rate control
choices.explanation: This does not address cardiac arrest.

choices.text: Routine synchronized cardioversion for a pulse-present rhythm
choices.explanation: The patient has no definite pulse.

ccu-lesson-05-dangerous-rhythms.point: An organized ECG does not exclude cardiac arrest.

ccu-lesson-06-electrical-treatment.stem: Which intervention is used for VF or pulseless VT arrest?

choices.text: Unsynchronized defibrillation
choices.explanation: These rhythms require a shockable arrest response.

choices.text: Synchronized cardioversion as the arrest default
choices.explanation: Synchronization is not the VF/pVT arrest shock mode.

choices.text: Routine transcutaneous pacing as the arrest default
choices.explanation: Pacing does not replace defibrillation for VF/pVT.

choices.text: Routine oral AV-nodal blockade
choices.explanation: This does not treat the arrest emergency.

ccu-lesson-06-electrical-treatment.point: Defibrillation is unsynchronized treatment for VF/pVT arrest.

ccu-lesson-06-electrical-treatment.stem: A patient has an unstable tachyarrhythmia with a pulse. Which electrical mode usually applies?

choices.text: Synchronized cardioversion
choices.explanation: The shock is timed to the R wave in the appropriate pulse-present rhythm.

choices.text: Unsynchronized shock as the rule for every pulse-present rhythm
choices.explanation: This ignores the synchronization requirement and specific exceptions.

choices.text: Transcutaneous pacing as the usual fast-rhythm treatment
choices.explanation: Pacing is used for dangerous bradycardia rather than this usual context.

choices.text: No electrical treatment until all biomarkers return
choices.explanation: Instability should not be delayed by routine laboratory results.

ccu-lesson-06-electrical-treatment.point: Synchronized cardioversion treats selected unstable tachyarrhythmia with a pulse.

ccu-lesson-06-electrical-treatment.stem: Why is a cardioversion shock synchronized to the R wave?

choices.text: To avoid shock delivery during vulnerable ventricular repolarization
choices.explanation: This reduces the risk of triggering a dangerous ventricular rhythm.

choices.text: To make shock energy depend on the atrial rate
choices.explanation: Synchronization selects timing, not energy based on atrial rate.

choices.text: To deliver pacing impulses between every pair of QRS complexes
choices.explanation: This describes neither a synchronized shock nor its purpose.

choices.text: To guarantee a pulse whenever a QRS is detected
choices.explanation: Electrical detection does not guarantee mechanical perfusion.

ccu-lesson-06-electrical-treatment.point: Synchronization avoids the vulnerable repolarization period.

ccu-lesson-06-electrical-treatment.stem: A critically unstable polymorphic VT requires a shock, but reliable synchronization is not possible. Which shock mode is appropriate?

choices.text: Unsynchronized shock
choices.explanation: Polymorphic VT cannot reliably support the usual R-wave synchronization.

choices.text: Repeatedly wait for a stable synchronization marker
choices.explanation: This can delay needed treatment.

choices.text: Routine pacing to create a marker first
choices.explanation: This is not the polymorphic VT shock response.

choices.text: A maintenance oral antiarrhythmic alone
choices.explanation: This does not address the immediate electrical emergency.

ccu-lesson-06-electrical-treatment.point: Polymorphic VT may require unsynchronized shock.

ccu-lesson-06-electrical-treatment.stem: Which problem is most appropriately treated with cardiac pacing?

choices.text: Dangerous symptomatic bradycardia or high-grade block
choices.explanation: Pacing provides repeated electrical stimulation when the effective rate is inadequate.

choices.text: VF arrest requiring defibrillation
choices.explanation: Pacing is not the shockable VF treatment.

choices.text: Stable sinus tachycardia after exertion
choices.explanation: This is not the dangerous slow-rhythm indication.

choices.text: An isolated normal ECG with no symptoms
choices.explanation: This does not establish a pacing indication.

ccu-lesson-06-electrical-treatment.point: Pacing supports dangerous symptomatic bradycardia/high-grade block.

ccu-lesson-06-electrical-treatment.stem: Pacing spikes are followed by QRS complexes, but the patient has no corresponding palpable pulse or BP response. What has not been established?

choices.text: Mechanical capture
choices.explanation: Electrical capture alone does not prove effective perfusion.

choices.text: Electrical capture
choices.explanation: A pacing spike followed by QRS supports electrical capture.

choices.text: The presence of a pacing spike
choices.explanation: Spikes are visible in the case.

choices.text: The presence of ventricular electrical activity
choices.explanation: QRS complexes establish that electrical finding.

ccu-lesson-06-electrical-treatment.stem: A patient has CHB, a very slow pulse, and poor perfusion. Which electrical preparation best matches the physiology?

choices.text: Pacing
choices.explanation: The problem is dangerous bradycardia with a pulse.

choices.text: Synchronized cardioversion for rapid SVT
choices.explanation: The rhythm is slow, not a tachyarrhythmia.

choices.text: Unsynchronized defibrillation for VF
choices.explanation: The patient has a pulse and an organized bradycardic rhythm.

choices.text: Shock avoidance based on ECG appearance alone
choices.explanation: The full clinical state requires urgent treatment preparation.

ccu-lesson-06-electrical-treatment.point: Choose electrical treatment from pulse status, rate, and stability.

ccu-lesson-06-electrical-treatment.stem: Which ECG finding indicates electrical capture during pacing?

choices.text: A pacing spike followed by a QRS complex
choices.explanation: This is electrical capture; the patient still needs a mechanical response check.

choices.text: A pacing spike without a following QRS complex
choices.explanation: A stimulus alone does not establish capture.

choices.text: A QRS complex with no temporal relationship to the pacing spike
choices.explanation: This does not demonstrate a paced response.

choices.text: A pacing spike followed by an isolated P wave without QRS
choices.explanation: This does not establish the ventricular electrical capture described.

ccu-lesson-06-electrical-treatment.point: Electrical capture is a pacing spike followed by a QRS complex.

ccu-lesson-07-sudden-deterioration.stem: A monitor alarm sounds as a CCU patient deteriorates. What should be assessed first?

choices.text: The patient’s responsiveness, airway, breathing, and circulation
choices.explanation: The monitor is interpreted alongside direct clinical assessment.

choices.text: The monitor’s diagnostic label without patient assessment
choices.explanation: A display does not establish the patient’s current physiological state.

choices.text: The routine medication-round sequence
choices.explanation: A new deterioration takes priority over routine sequencing.

choices.text: The previous shift’s stable observations alone
choices.explanation: Earlier stability does not establish the current condition.

ccu-lesson-07-sudden-deterioration.point: Assess the patient and ABCs before relying on the monitor label.

ccu-lesson-07-sudden-deterioration.stem: Which observation belongs primarily to the Disability component of an ABCDE assessment?

choices.text: Consciousness or new confusion
choices.explanation: Disability includes neurological state.

choices.text: Airway obstruction
choices.explanation: This belongs to Airway.

choices.text: Respiratory effort
choices.explanation: This belongs to Breathing.

choices.text: Pulse and skin perfusion
choices.explanation: These belong to Circulation.

ccu-lesson-07-sudden-deterioration.point: Use focused ABCDE assessment to identify immediate problems.

ccu-lesson-07-sudden-deterioration.stem: Which change is a clear warning of clinical deterioration?

choices.text: New confusion with a marked BP fall
choices.explanation: Both are red flags for impaired perfusion or another acute problem.

choices.text: Improved breathing with stable BP
choices.explanation: This describes improvement rather than the warning pattern.

choices.text: Pain improving without new symptoms
choices.explanation: This does not identify acute deterioration.

choices.text: An unchanged chronic symptom with stable observations
choices.explanation: No acute warning change is described.

ccu-lesson-07-sudden-deterioration.stem: After an intervention for sudden deterioration, what establishes whether it has helped?

choices.text: Repeat relevant clinical observations and compare the response
choices.explanation: Response must be assessed rather than inferred from treatment being given.

choices.text: The fact that the intervention was prescribed
choices.explanation: A correct order does not establish effectiveness in this patient.

choices.text: The completion of a medication chart entry alone
choices.explanation: Documentation alone does not measure response.

choices.text: The patient’s observations from the previous day alone
choices.explanation: These are not a current post-intervention assessment.

ccu-lesson-07-sudden-deterioration.stem: A previously monitored patient is now unresponsive, not breathing normally, and has no definite pulse after a prompt check. Which response has priority?

choices.text: Activate the arrest response and begin resuscitation
choices.explanation: Pulseless deterioration requires immediate action.

choices.text: Obtain a routine 12-lead before starting the arrest response
choices.explanation: A diagnostic tracing must not delay resuscitation.

choices.text: Complete a full medication reconciliation first
choices.explanation: This is secondary to immediate life support.

choices.text: Wait for a laboratory explanation before treating the collapse
choices.explanation: A possible cause does not justify delaying resuscitation.

ccu-lesson-07-sudden-deterioration.point: Treat a pulseless unresponsive patient as an arrest.

ccu-lesson-07-sudden-deterioration.stem: A CCU patient has rapidly worsening dyspnea, falling oxygen saturation, and confusion. Which response is most appropriate?

choices.text: Assess ABCs, obtain current observations, support as indicated, and escalate
choices.explanation: The clinical deterioration requires simultaneous assessment, support, and help.

choices.text: Complete routine discharge education before reassessment
choices.explanation: This delays response to acute instability.

choices.text: Repeat the previous stable observation values in the chart
choices.explanation: Current findings must be measured and reported.

choices.text: Treat the monitor reading without checking breathing or circulation
choices.explanation: Direct patient assessment remains essential.

ccu-lesson-07-sudden-deterioration.point: Prepare support while escalating an evolving respiratory/perfusion problem.

ccu-lesson-07-sudden-deterioration.stem: VT appears on telemetry. Which current bedside information immediately determines the major treatment pathway?

choices.text: Pulse presence and clinical perfusion
choices.explanation: This distinguishes arrest from a stable or unstable pulse-present problem.

choices.text: The previous ECG axis and R-wave progression
choices.explanation: Earlier electrical characteristics do not establish current circulation.

choices.text: The last troponin value and planned sampling time
choices.explanation: Biomarkers must not delay current pulse and perfusion assessment.

choices.text: The previous antiarrhythmic dose and its routine due time
choices.explanation: Medication history matters but does not replace the current circulation assessment.

ccu-lesson-07-sudden-deterioration.point: A dangerous monitor pattern needs immediate patient and pulse correlation.

ccu-lesson-07-sudden-deterioration.stem: Which focused observation belongs to Exposure in the rapid ABCDE assessment?

choices.text: Visible bleeding and an abnormal line site
choices.explanation: These are visible potential causes assessed under Exposure.

choices.text: The ability to speak through a clear airway
choices.explanation: This primarily assesses Airway.

choices.text: Respiratory effort and breath sounds
choices.explanation: These primarily assess Breathing.

choices.text: New confusion and reduced responsiveness
choices.explanation: These primarily assess Disability.

ccu-lesson-07-sudden-deterioration.point: Exposure assessment includes bleeding, lines, edema, and visible causes.

choices.text: Insufficient cardiac pumping to perfuse organs
choices.explanation: The primary problem is a weak pump and inadequate effective output.

choices.text: An empty intravascular tank as the primary mechanism
choices.explanation: That describes hypovolemic shock.

choices.text: Pathological vasodilation as the primary mechanism
choices.explanation: That describes a distributive pattern.

choices.text: Mechanical obstruction to flow as the primary mechanism
choices.explanation: That describes an obstructive pattern.

ccu-lesson-08-cardiogenic-shock.point: Cardiogenic shock is pump failure with organ hypoperfusion.

ccu-lesson-08-cardiogenic-shock.stem: Which cluster supports concern about inadequate organ perfusion?

choices.text: Cold skin, weak pulses, confusion, and low urine output
choices.explanation: These are indicators of hypoperfusion.

choices.text: Normal alertness with improving urine output
choices.explanation: This is more consistent with improvement.

choices.text: Warm comfortable skin with stable mentation alone
choices.explanation: This does not establish the low-output cluster.

choices.text: A normal pain score with no other findings
choices.explanation: Pain severity does not establish adequate organ perfusion.

ccu-lesson-08-cardiogenic-shock.stem: Which event most directly provides a pump-failure explanation for shock?

choices.text: Acute MI with markedly impaired ventricular contraction
choices.explanation: Myocardial injury can reduce output.

choices.text: Major gastrointestinal blood loss with reduced circulating volume
choices.explanation: This primarily supports a hypovolemic mechanism.

choices.text: Severe infection with predominant loss of vascular tone
choices.explanation: This primarily supports a distributive mechanism.

choices.text: A massive pulmonary embolus obstructing forward flow
choices.explanation: This primarily supports an obstructive mechanism.

ccu-lesson-08-cardiogenic-shock.point: MI, severe HF, arrhythmia, and mechanical problems can impair the pump.

ccu-lesson-08-cardiogenic-shock.stem: A hypotensive patient has crackles and suspected pump failure. What is the main concern with assuming a large fluid bolus is appropriate?

choices.text: Added filling load may worsen pulmonary edema
choices.explanation: A failing pump may not handle the extra volume.

choices.text: Added fluid consistently lowers cardiac filling pressure
choices.explanation: This reverses the immediate loading effect.

choices.text: Added fluid directly corrects the loss of myocardial contractility
choices.explanation: Volume is not an inotrope.

choices.text: Added fluid reliably distinguishes cardiogenic from hypovolemic shock
choices.explanation: The whole clinical picture must guide the authorized plan.

ccu-lesson-08-cardiogenic-shock.point: A large automatic fluid bolus may worsen pulmonary edema in pump failure.

ccu-lesson-08-cardiogenic-shock.stem: Patient A has hypotension, raised JVP, and crackles after MI. Patient B has hypotension after major fluid loss, flat neck veins, and clear lungs. Which comparison fits?

choices.text: A suggests cardiogenic; B suggests hypovolemic shock
choices.explanation: The congestion and volume-loss contexts support different mechanisms.

choices.text: A suggests hypovolemic; B suggests cardiogenic shock
choices.explanation: This reverses the principal patterns.

choices.text: Both are established as distributive solely from low BP
choices.explanation: Hypotension alone does not identify the mechanism.

choices.text: Both are established as obstructive solely from low BP
choices.explanation: The cases do not provide that common mechanism.

ccu-lesson-08-cardiogenic-shock.point: Differentiate pump failure from volume-loss patterns using the full picture.

ccu-lesson-08-cardiogenic-shock.stem: Which pair correctly matches a shock type to its mechanism?

choices.text: Distributive: excessive dilation; obstructive: blocked flow
choices.explanation: These are the non-pump mechanisms.

choices.text: Distributive: empty tank; obstructive: weak contraction
choices.explanation: Those describe different primary mechanisms.

choices.text: Cardiogenic: empty tank; hypovolemic: blocked flow
choices.explanation: This reverses the principal definitions.

choices.text: Hypovolemic: excessive dilation; cardiogenic: blocked flow
choices.explanation: This misidentifies both mechanisms.

ccu-lesson-08-cardiogenic-shock.point: Recognize distributive and obstructive shock mechanisms.

ccu-lesson-08-cardiogenic-shock.stem: During treatment, BP improves but confusion, cool skin, and oliguria persist. Which conclusion is most defensible?

choices.text: Perfusion remains concerning despite a better BP
choices.explanation: Multiple organ indicators must improve before response is assumed.

choices.text: The BP improvement establishes complete recovery
choices.explanation: Persistent organ findings contradict that inference.

choices.text: Oliguria establishes successful decongestion by itself
choices.explanation: Low output does not establish a beneficial treatment response.

choices.text: Cool skin excludes ongoing shock
choices.explanation: Coolness can be a hypoperfusion sign.

ccu-lesson-08-cardiogenic-shock.point: A BP value must be interpreted with organ perfusion.

ccu-lesson-09-norepi-dobutamine.stem: Which primary role best describes norepinephrine in this comparison?

choices.text: Increase vascular tone and support pressure
choices.explanation: It is primarily a vasopressor.

choices.text: Reduce platelet aggregation
choices.explanation: That is an antiplatelet role.

choices.text: Block the gastric proton pump
choices.explanation: That is an acid-suppression role.

choices.text: Increase renal glucose excretion
choices.explanation: That is an SGLT2-inhibitor role.

ccu-lesson-09-norepi-dobutamine.point: Norepinephrine primarily supports vascular tone and pressure.

ccu-lesson-09-norepi-dobutamine.stem: Which primary role best describes dobutamine?

choices.text: Increase cardiac contractility and output
choices.explanation: It primarily supports the pump.

choices.text: Reduce cardiac contractility through beta1 blockade
choices.explanation: This is the opposite adrenergic action.

choices.text: Suppress gastric acid through proton-pump blockade
choices.explanation: This is a PPI action.

choices.text: Inhibit platelet P2Y12 receptors
choices.explanation: This is an antiplatelet action.

ccu-lesson-09-norepi-dobutamine.point: Dobutamine primarily supports contractility and output.

ccu-lesson-09-norepi-dobutamine.stem: A patient has both inadequate contractility and dangerously low arterial pressure. Why might the team prescribe both medicines?

choices.text: They address different components of the hemodynamic problem
choices.explanation: Dobutamine supports contractility while norepinephrine supports vascular pressure.

choices.text: They are identical drugs with different trade names
choices.explanation: They have distinct pharmacological roles.

choices.text: They both work by inhibiting cardiac beta1 receptors
choices.explanation: Both are not beta1 antagonists.

choices.text: They replace the need to monitor clinical perfusion
choices.explanation: Vasoactive treatment increases the need for monitoring.

ccu-lesson-09-norepi-dobutamine.point: Pressure and pump support may be combined.

ccu-lesson-09-norepi-dobutamine.stem: Which group best evaluates the response and safety of these vasoactive infusions?

choices.text: BP, rhythm, perfusion, and urine output
choices.explanation: These follow hemodynamic response and potential adverse effects.

choices.text: INR, tablet count, and diet history alone
choices.explanation: These do not establish the immediate infusion response.

choices.text: Stool color, bowel frequency, and oral lesions alone
choices.explanation: These do not assess the principal hemodynamic effects.

choices.text: Wound length, suture count, and joint range alone
choices.explanation: These address another clinical domain.

ccu-lesson-09-norepi-dobutamine.point: Monitor rhythm, pressure, urine output, and peripheral perfusion.

ccu-lesson-09-norepi-dobutamine.stem: A norepinephrine bag is changed to twice the concentration while the required dose is unchanged. What mL/hour change gives the same drug amount?

choices.text: Half the previous mL/hour
choices.explanation: Doubling concentration halves the volume needed for the same dose.

choices.text: Twice the previous mL/hour
choices.explanation: This would deliver four times the prior drug amount.

choices.text: The same mL/hour
choices.explanation: This would double the delivered drug amount.

choices.text: Four times the previous mL/hour
choices.explanation: This would cause a still larger drug delivery increase.

ccu-lesson-09-norepi-dobutamine.point: mL/hour depends on the ordered dose and prepared concentration.

ccu-lesson-09-norepi-dobutamine.explanation: 4 divided by 8 is 0.5 mL/min; multiply by 60 for 30 mL/hour.

ccu-lesson-09-norepi-dobutamine.stem: BP improves during peripheral norepinephrine, but the IV site becomes painful, pale, and cool. What is the best interpretation?

choices.text: A local infusion complication can coexist with systemic pressure benefit
choices.explanation: Assess and escalate the threatened site promptly.

choices.text: The BP improvement establishes local tissue safety
choices.explanation: Systemic response does not exclude local ischemia/extravasation.

choices.text: Local pallor establishes that the entire circulating volume has fallen
choices.explanation: The local signs require a site-focused assessment.

choices.text: Local pain is evidence that the prescribed dose is too low
choices.explanation: The site change is not a valid reason to increase the infusion.

ccu-lesson-09-norepi-dobutamine.point: Norepinephrine monitoring includes peripheral IV site ischemia/extravasation signs.

ccu-lesson-10-electrolytes.stem: Which ECG pattern is compatible with low potassium?

choices.text: Flattened T waves or U waves
choices.explanation: These can accompany hypokalemia and ectopy.

choices.text: A shortened QT as the main calcium pattern
choices.explanation: This relates to a different electrolyte effect.

choices.text: A pacing spike followed by a captured QRS
choices.explanation: This describes pacing rather than potassium status.

choices.text: Independent atrial and ventricular rates alone
choices.explanation: This identifies a conduction relationship, not a specific low-potassium pattern.

ccu-lesson-10-electrolytes.point: Low potassium can cause flat T waves/U waves and arrhythmia.

ccu-lesson-10-electrolytes.stem: A patient with high potassium develops progressive QRS widening and bradycardia. What does the ECG change indicate?

choices.text: Potentially dangerous electrical toxicity needing urgent escalation
choices.explanation: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes is a time-critical problem.

choices.text: A reliable sign of improved potassium clearance
choices.explanation: Worsening conduction is not evidence of successful correction.

choices.text: An isolated artifact established by the potassium result
choices.explanation: A known electrolyte problem does not make the ECG change artifact.

choices.text: An expected therapeutic pacing response
choices.explanation: No pacing intervention is described.

ccu-lesson-10-electrolytes.point: Severe high potassium can widen QRS and produce bradyarrhythmia/arrest.

ccu-lesson-10-electrolytes.stem: Why is magnesium relevant when hypokalemia is difficult to correct?

choices.text: Low magnesium can make potassium correction harder
choices.explanation: These findings have a clinically important relationship.

choices.text: Magnesium directly replaces potassium ion for ion
choices.explanation: They are different electrolytes.

choices.text: Normal magnesium eliminates every arrhythmia cause
choices.explanation: Rhythm problems have multiple possible causes.

choices.text: Low magnesium reliably shortens the potassium treatment course
choices.explanation: Deficiency can interfere with correction rather than reliably shorten it.

ccu-lesson-10-electrolytes.point: Low magnesium can contribute to ventricular arrhythmia and refractory hypokalemia.

ccu-lesson-10-electrolytes.stem: Which pairing correctly relates calcium level to the QT interval?

choices.text: Low calcium: longer QT; high calcium: shorter QT
choices.explanation: The direction of the QT effect differs with calcium status.

choices.text: Low calcium: shorter QT; high calcium: longer QT
choices.explanation: This reverses the relationship.

choices.text: Low calcium: no QT effect; high calcium: no QT effect
choices.explanation: Calcium influences ventricular repolarization.

choices.text: Low calcium: pacing capture; high calcium: AV dissociation
choices.explanation: Those are not calcium/QT definitions.

ccu-lesson-10-electrolytes.point: Calcium affects QT in opposite directions when low or high.

ccu-lesson-10-electrolytes.stem: A patient receiving a loop diuretic develops new ventricular ectopy. Which investigation pair best checks for a medication-related electrolyte cause?

choices.text: Potassium and magnesium
choices.explanation: Diuretic-associated losses can contribute to ventricular irritability.

choices.text: Albumin and bilirubin
choices.explanation: These do not best assess the immediate electrolyte-linked rhythm issue.

choices.text: Amylase and lipase
choices.explanation: These assess a different organ system.

choices.text: TSH and thyroxine
choices.explanation: Thyroid testing does not best target the acute loop-diuretic loss context.

ccu-lesson-10-electrolytes.point: Loop-diuretic-associated PVCs warrant potassium and magnesium review.

ccu-lesson-10-electrolytes.stem: Which method of potassium administration is unsafe?

choices.text: Rapid IV push
choices.explanation: Concentrated rapid IV potassium can cause fatal cardiac effects.

choices.text: A verified protocol-controlled infusion
choices.explanation: Properly prescribed controlled infusion is a different method.

choices.text: An authorized oral dose when indicated
choices.explanation: Oral treatment is not the rapid-IV-push hazard.

choices.text: A prescribed and monitored replacement plan
choices.explanation: The prohibition concerns uncontrolled rapid IV administration.

ccu-lesson-10-electrolytes.point: Never give IV potassium as a rapid IV push.

ccu-lesson-10-electrolytes.stem: A patient has recurrent torsades de pointes. Which electrolyte is specifically important in its treatment?

choices.text: Magnesium
choices.explanation: Magnesium is important in the treatment of torsades.

choices.text: Sodium
choices.explanation: This is not the specifically highlighted torsades electrolyte.

choices.text: Phosphate
choices.explanation: This is not the specifically highlighted torsades electrolyte.

choices.text: Chloride
choices.explanation: This is not the specifically highlighted torsades electrolyte.

ccu-lesson-10-electrolytes.point: Magnesium is important in torsades de pointes.

ccu-lesson-11-furosemide.stem: Which presentation most directly supports the use of furosemide?

choices.text: Breathlessness, crackles, and edema from congestion
choices.explanation: The loop diuretic helps remove excess fluid.

choices.text: Isolated low glucose requiring immediate replacement
choices.explanation: Furosemide does not supply glucose.

choices.text: An isolated mechanical bowel obstruction
choices.explanation: This is not the diuretic indication.

choices.text: An isolated oral fungal infection
choices.explanation: This requires a different treatment.

ccu-lesson-11-furosemide.point: Furosemide treats congestion and fluid overload.

ccu-lesson-11-furosemide.stem: Which effect links furosemide to reduced congestion?

choices.text: Increased salt and water excretion
choices.explanation: Diuresis reduces excess fluid burden.

choices.text: Increased platelet aggregation
choices.explanation: This is not the decongestive mechanism.
